transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… I guess I’m here because I keep having these doubts that I can’t quite shake. I know everyone double-checks things, and I don’t want to make it sound more dramatic than it is, but I’ll check something—like a mortgage payment number, or a clause in a client proof, or whether a door is really latched—and even after I’ve checked it, the thought comes back. Like, “What if this is the one mistake that costs you everything?” It’s… hard to get past, even when part of me knows I already looked.
Do these thoughts ever feel intrusive or unwanted, like they don’t really fit with how you see yourself, and do they cause you a lot of anxiety or discomfort?

Yes… I think that’s fair to say. I mean, I don’t want to overstate it, but they do feel unwanted. It’s not like I’m trying to worry about these things.

It’s more like the doubt barges in after I’ve already checked—like, what if I missed a number on the mortgage payment, or didn’t catch something in a client proof, or the door isn’t actually latched. And then my mind goes straight to, “What if this is the mistake that costs you everything?” It feels… out of proportion, I know that, but it still makes me really anxious.
When these doubts come up, do you find yourself doing something over and over—like checking things again, repeating a phrase in your head, or trying to neutralize the thought in some way?

Yes… I do, though I feel a little embarrassed saying it. It’s not anything dramatic, I guess, but I’ll reopen files after I’ve already checked them, reread emails several times, or go back to the online payment confirmation just to make sure the number is really right.

And sometimes I’ll sort of… say the figures silently in my head until they feel settled, if that makes sense. Like I know I’ve seen them, but they don’t feel okay yet. It can turn something simple, like an invoice or a logo revision, into hours, and then I can’t really bill for that time. I know that probably sounds inefficient.
How much do these thoughts and the things you do to manage them interfere with your day-to-day life—like your work, your relationships, or the amount of time you spend on tasks?

It does interfere, more than I’d like to admit. I mean, I still get things done, mostly, so I don’t want to make it sound like I’m completely falling apart. But work that used to take me an afternoon can drag on for days because I keep checking and revising and making sure I haven’t missed something.

I’ve missed billable hours because I can’t really charge a client for all that extra checking, and I’ve had to push back deadlines. One longtime client has even asked whether I can still handle simple revisions on time, which was… hard to hear. I know that probably answers your question.

Are there other thoughts, images, or urges that bother you in a similar way, or things you feel you have to do repeatedly to reduce anxiety, even if they’re not related to checking work or making sure things are secure?

I’m not sure… I don’t think so, at least not in the same clear way. Most of what I notice is tied to making sure I haven’t made a mistake or left something undone.

I mean, I do worry generally, but I don’t know that I have other specific images or urges like you’re describing. If there’s something in particular you mean, I can think about it, but nothing else is really coming to mind right now.
Do these worries or checking behaviors ever spill over into other parts of your life—like your relationships, home life, or things you used to enjoy doing?

Yes… mostly with work, I’d say. I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is, but it has had a real effect there.

I’ve missed billable hours because I can’t really charge people for all the extra checking, and I’ve pushed deadlines back when something that used to take an afternoon stretches into days. One client I’ve worked with for a long time even asked if I could still manage simple revisions on time, which was pretty upsetting.

So, I guess… yes, it does spill over in the sense that work is my day-to-day life. I’m not sure if that’s the kind of thing you mean.
